Source: http://www.press.co.nz/

Posted March 14, 2000
(MarijuanaNews note: This is another example of how prohibitionism works as an international ideology. An American academic’s work on Dutch marijuana use is misreported by the AP and then completely misrepresented by the DEAland Drug Czar, who should not be citing wire stories, in the first place. This is then quoted by a New Zealand prohibitionist, who should know better, given his position of " trust. ".)

March 13, 2000
From The New Zealand Press
editorial@press.co.nz
http://www.press.co.nz/
Letter to the editor from Jeff McIntyre, Chairman of The Youth Trust

DUTCH STRATEGY LEADS TO INCREASED CANNABIS USE
Sir-
McCouns’ study comparison of Dutch cannabis use with its prohibiting neighbours showed depenalisation led to increased cannabis use compared with those countries.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, this is the exact opposite of what MacCoun said. In a letter to the San Francisco Examiner, dated October 13, 1997, MacCoun said, " In recent years, levels of use have also grown steeply in other countries with very different policies, including our own. Furthermore, we argued that data from both the Netherlands and the United States suggest that it is possible to stop imprisoning cannabis users without producing detectable increases in cannabis use. " )

The US Monitoring the Future survey reported regular cannabis use by high school seniors dropped from 37 per cent in 1979 to 12 per cent in 1992. This was achieved by an inter-agency effort involving schools, communities, social workers, police, courts, excellent treatment options, and prohibition.
(MarijuanaNews note: And this is also untrue, but it is a quote of a lie told by the Czar.)
See
Drug Czar’s Office Issues New " Fact Sheet " On " The Drug Situation in the Netherlands "
and numerous links.

Prohibition by itself does not work. Just because our current approach fails, why move to a model that will increase use and the obvious harm that is particularly noticeable with adolescent use?

Decriminalisation will reduce prices but that does not mean gangs will disappear. They will switch their efforts to more profitable, harder drugs and New Zealand will be flooded with heroin, like Australia. Soon we will be arguing, like the Australians are, about legalising heroin.

(MarijuanaNews note: Then why is the Dutch rate of heroin use so low?)

(MarijuanaNews note: The following offers even more insight into how reefer madness is perpetuated.)

Excerpt From 8/11/99 email from Rob MacCoun to cowan@marijuananews.com

I was browsing through your interesting web page and found the reference to the Associated Press distortion of our findings in our 1997 Science article.

For the record, this is a mistake by Paul Recer (at AP), not by me. He juxtaposed a quote from me about the Netherlands with his own misleading comparison.

Our correction letter was sent to every paper that ran the story. Only the Honolulu Advertiser published our letter.

(MarijuanaNews note: Many papers ran the error, but only one ran the correction!)
The letter stated:

" We are writing to correct two errors in the October 3rd story describing our study on the effects of the Dutch cannabis policy.

First, Dutch cannabis prices ranges from $2 to $12 per gram, not per joint. Second, the story noted that " the percentage of 18-year-olds who had tried marijuana rose from 15 percent to 44 percent " in the Netherlands, but " by contrast, teenage use of marijuana in the United States was estimated at about 12 percent in 1992. " This comparison, which is not taken from our article (Science, Oct. 3), is quite misleading, for two reasons.

First, it compares the lifetime experience of Dutch 18-year-olds to that of all US teens. But in each country, 18-year-olds are much more likely to have tried marijuana than other teens, because they have lived longer, and because drug experimentation is more common in late adolescence.

Second, it compares a 1996 Dutch rate with a 1992 US rate, yet US rates skyrocketed between 1992 and 1996. In 1992, 34 percent of Dutch 18-year-olds had tried cannabis; the comparable figure for American 18-year-olds was 33 percent.

In 1996, the rates were 44 percent and 45 percent, respectively. "
(MarijuanaNews note: The Dutch numbers that MacCoun cites are a bit higher than those that I have found, but the point remains the same, marijuana prohibition does not lower teen marijuana use rates.)

Best wishes,

Rob MacCoun
Goldman School of Pub Policy
Univ. Calif. at Berkeley
